Photo by Towfiqu barbhuiya on UnsplashAn AI tutor will never give you the social stakes of a real conversation. There’s no fear of being laughed at, no reward for landing a joke in a second language, no stranger deciding whether you’re worth the effort of slowing down for. That’s not a flaw to be engineered away. It’s the category.
An AI tutor is a gym. The point of the gym is to make the match survivable.
Which means the question isn’t “can it replace a human tutor?” It can’t. The question is whether it’s a good gym or a room with mirrors. Most people picture an AI language tutor as a chatbot that compliments your typos, and that image is a few years out of date. It also makes learners skip the most patient teacher they have access to.
I’ve built one of these: OwnSlides, which has a text and voice tutor. So rather than argue in the abstract, here are five tests. Each takes about two minutes. Run them on whatever tool you’re evaluating, mine included. I’ll point out where OwnSlides does something specific, and where the problem is just genuinely hard for everyone.
Test 1: Say something slightly beyond your level. Does the difficulty move?
What to do: Answer two or three questions in the most confident, complex sentences you can manage. Then, deliberately, stall — give a one-word answer, or say you don’t understand.
What good looks like: The difficulty climbs when you’re fluent and drops when you stall, and it never announces itself. You shouldn’t see the machinery. You should only notice that the conversation stays slightly harder than comfortable.
What it means if it fails: A tutor that talks to a beginner in native-speed idioms is showing off. One that talks to a B2 learner like a toddler has stopped paying attention. Both are the same failure — a fixed difficulty that ignores you.
That band of “slightly too hard” has a name in learning science. Lev Vygotsky called it the zone of proximal development: the range between what you can do alone and what you can do with help. It’s where the learning actually happens. Too easy is entertainment. Too hard is noise.
Building this into OwnSlides was harder than I expected, and the reason is instructive: the tutor has to infer your level from very little evidence, early, and be willing to revise that guess mid-conversation. Get it wrong in the confident direction and you drown a beginner. Get it wrong in the cautious direction and you bore someone who was ready for more.
Test 2: Make a real mistake. Does practice follow the mistake, or the schedule?
What to do: Mix up two tenses mid-conversation. Use the wrong preposition twice. Then keep talking and see what the tool does with it.
What good looks like: The conversation spawns a short, targeted drill on exactly that confusion — then returns to the conversation. Brief, earned, specific.
What it means if it fails: There are two opposite failure modes here, and most tools pick one. Language apps default to the endless quiz: tap the matching card, fill the blank, collect the confetti, none of it connected to anything you actually got wrong. Pure chatbots default to the opposite — pleasant, frictionless talk with no pressure to produce anything precise. You leave feeling good and nothing sticks.
The format of the exercise matters much less than its trigger. Practice should respond to your errors, not arrive on a timer.
In OwnSlides this is the piece I’ve rewritten most often. The tutor generates the drill from the mistake you just made, which sounds obvious and is a genuine engineering problem — you’re deciding, live, whether an error is worth interrupting for, then building a two-minute exercise around it, then getting back to the conversation before the thread goes cold.
Test 3: Say something understandable but imperfect. Does it interrupt you?
What to do: Drop an article. Get a gender wrong. Say something that’s clearly comprehensible and clearly not correct — then watch whether it addresses your point or your grammar first.
What good looks like: It answers what you said. Then it circles back with one small correction. Errors that block communication get fixed immediately; errors of polish get noted and drilled later. That’s triage, and it’s what a good human tutor does automatically.
What it means if it fails: If it stops the conversation over a missing article, it’s optimising for looking smart rather than for you getting better.
This isn’t a style preference. Lyster and Ranta’s classic study of French immersion classrooms found that the most common teacher move — the recast, quietly repeating your sentence back in corrected form — was also the least likely to produce any actual repair from the student. Correction that’s frictionless to deliver is often the kind that doesn’t land. Separately, work on foreign language anxiety has long linked harsh or relentless correction to learners withdrawing from speaking at all. A silent learner learns nothing.
Test 4: Come back tomorrow. Does it remember today?
What to do: Have a session. Note two or three words you struggled with. Come back the next day and see whether they surface.
What good looks like: Thursday’s conversation is shaped by Tuesday’s difficulties. The words you fumbled come back — in a review deck, in a drill, or just seeded into the next conversation.
What it means if it fails: A session that starts from zero every time is a demo, not a tutor. Memory is also what makes progress visible, and visible progress is what keeps the habit alive when motivation dips. A skills chart moving, a review deck growing, an accuracy trend going the right way — those aren’t gamification garnish. They’re the reason you open the app on day forty.
OwnSlides handles this by pushing words you’ve struggled with into a spaced-repetition deck, so they come back at widening intervals rather than at random. That’s a well-understood technique and not remotely unique to me — but it does require the tutor to be writing things down about you during the conversation, which is the part a stateless chatbot structurally cannot do.
Test 5: Ask it what you’re bad at. Does it have an answer?
What to do: Straightforwardly ask: what am I struggling with?
What good looks like: A specific answer. “Past-tense endings” or “you avoid the subjunctive” — something derived from what you’ve actually done, that you could act on today.
What it means if it fails: Vague encouragement means it isn’t tracking anything. “You’re doing great, keep practising!” is what a tool says when there’s no model of you underneath it. If it can’t tell you what you’re bad at, it can’t be building anything around your weaknesses either — and Tests 1, 2 and 4 were all quietly depending on that model existing.
The shape of a good session
(Illustrative — this is the pattern the tests above are describing, not a transcript of any particular product.)
You: Yesterday I go to the market and buy some fish.
Tutor: Nice — what kind of fish? Anything you hadn’t cooked before?
You: Is a fish called dorada. I never cook it before.
Tutor: Dorada’s a good one — sea bream. Quick thing before you tell me how it turned out: you said “I go” and “I never cook it.” Both should be past. Try that first sentence again?
You: Yesterday I went to the market and bought some fish.
Tutor: That’s it. So — how did the dorada turn out?
Four things happened there. The tutor answered the content before the grammar. It let the first error pass to keep the conversation moving, then caught the pattern when it repeated. The correction was one line, not a lecture. And the conversation resumed exactly where it left off.
That’s the whole thing. Everything else is interface.
Frequently asked
Can an AI tutor replace a human one? No, and the useful version of that answer is specific: it can’t replicate social stakes, cultural nuance, or the accountability of a person expecting you on Thursday. What it can do is give you unlimited, unembarrassing repetition — which is exactly what most learners are short of between human sessions.
Is talking to an AI actually useful if it never gets impatient? That’s the trade. Infinite patience is why you’ll say things to it you’d be too self-conscious to attempt with a person. It also means the pressure has to come from the tool’s design — difficulty that climbs, corrections that land — rather than from social risk. That’s what Tests 1 and 3 are checking for.
How much does this beat just using a general-purpose chatbot? For pure conversation practice, a general chatbot does fine. It fails Tests 4 and 5 — no memory across sessions, no model of your weaknesses — so it can’t build anything cumulative. If you only ever want to talk, that may not matter to you.
What this all costs you if you get it wrong
Nothing dramatic — that’s the problem. A bad AI tutor doesn’t fail loudly. It gives you a pleasant twenty minutes a day, a streak counter, and a slowly growing certainty that you’re not really improving. The tests above take ten minutes total and will tell you inside the first session which one you’ve got.
I build OwnSlides — text and voice tutoring built along exactly these lines, because these are the things I kept wanting and not finding. Run the five tests on it. Run them on whatever else you’re considering. If a product fails them, the logo doesn’t matter.
